scores.title: FLIPSIDE
scores.strengths: Best hook of the five. The first frame is tactile, ASMR-like macro sequins with glints. At 1.8 s one tile does a springy flip, and at 2.4 s a line of flips races away like falling dominoes. It feels like a satisfying-loop clip, then shows it is not one, and the viewer has a reason to stay before 3 s. The scale reveal comes at 3.5-6 s, early enough for social. The sequin-desert-to-cobalt-ocean flip-front on the drop (8.5 s) gives the most quotable frame here: a split frame, tangerine dunes on one side and cobalt swells on the other, divided by a rolling front of flipping tiles. Every twist uses one object, so 'impossible, then obvious' really works. The rule-breaks escalate: scale, then solid to liquid, then rock to flock to forest, then world to object. Tangerine against cobalt, with magenta and chartreuse accents, is the most saturated and graphic palette of the five and is very far from teal and gold. The seamless lid-flip loop invites a rewatch. Nothing about it suggests a temple build reel.
scores.weaknesses: It packs five rule-breaks into 30 s, so it risks reading as a montage of tricks with no room to breathe. The murmuration-to-jacaranda segment (14-20.5 s) is the most likely to read as a glittery blob. Trees built from tiles sampled off a Poly Haven mesh may look lumpy. The blinking giant eye on the planet is the cheesiest beat in any concept: cute or cringe, nothing in between. The biggest technical threat to looking premium is sub-pixel specular shimmer from hundreds of thousands of thin-film metal mirrors at 24 fps in EEVEE. If it flickers, the whole 'clean as hell' brief fails. From 25 m out, the far field is shader-faked glitter carpet that can look like noise. Three scene scales plus a separate planet scene make it a heavy build.

scores.title: NEEDLE DROP
scores.strengths: Strong first 2 seconds: a fast skim down a glossy magenta and ultramarine marbled canyon, with motion and saturated colour from frame 1. Its first surprise (the groove is a record, and the walls are the soundtrack you are hearing) lands at 4.2 s, which is ideal timing for social. Every motion is locked to the real track through the spectrum EXR and beat grid, which gives it motion-studio precision viewers feel even if they can't name it. The cymatic desert that self-organises into a vinyl record seen top-down is a genuinely original and memorable image. A mountain-sized chrome tonearm lowering out of the sky, landing on the same needle-drop crackle that opens the film, is a great payoff and loop.
scores.weaknesses: Six different worlds in 30 s (groove, turntable, wire, city, cone, desert), each 3-6 s, so it plays like a sizzle reel and each set gets less polish. The middle is cliché. The inside-the-wire light tunnel is Tron or hyperspace. A skyline where every tower is an EQ band is one of the most overused audio-visualiser tropes. Speaker-cone slams are stock music-video imagery. The 'journey of the signal' structure is a familiar ad format (Powers-of-Ten-style audio-brand spots), so the overall concept is less surprising than its best moments. The turntable product shot (6-10.5 s) is a lull in energy. Six separate builds is a lot for one night of AI iteration.

scores.title: ONESIDE
scores.strengths: Has the most genuinely mind-bending single ideas. The sun sets because the ground rolls over (6-9 s), with a razor shadow line sweeping like a clock hand. The river does not fall off the edge of the world but wraps around the rim, and the camera curls with it from midnight to noon in 1.8 s. 'The sky is land' at 3-4.5 s is a strong early jolt. Day and night as places rather than times is a smart concept that rewards a rewatch, and the seamless loop is well engineered. The day palette (chartreuse, coral, magenta, cobalt) is very far from the reference.
scores.weaknesses: The first 2 seconds are a generic grass-blade meadow with flowers, a weak scroll-stopper, and rising pollen is too subtle to read as a hook. The corkscrew world-roll will most likely read to viewers as a camera barrel-roll, not as the world turning, so the key surprise may not land. A ringworld or Möbius world from 5 km out sits close to Halo, Elysium and Escher imagery, and it can read as a twisted toy ribbon. It has the heaviest environment build: millions of grass instances, recoloured Poly Haven flora, a night set and a day set. That is exactly where AI-built Blender scenes slide into a generic Poly Haven landscape look. The maglev is visual filler rather than an idea.

scores.title: RANGE
scores.strengths: Elegant single-object concept that an AI can build very precisely: one pencil mesh repeated 288 times, with real lacquer, primer seam, growth rings and facet ridges. The craft ceiling is high. The pull-back that reveals the sky as a paper sweep and the sun as an LED panel is a nice second layer. The music-driven ripple of pencils with a unison jump, a one-frame hang and a slam is satisfying. The final stroke turning out to be the opening skyline is a clever loop. Using the change of DOF to tell the scale change is smart craft. Palette and subject are clean and unrelated to the reference.
scores.weaknesses: The whole film rests on a reveal at 10.8 s, which is far too late for social. A sharpened coloured-pencil tip (steep, uniform 20-degree wood cone with a coloured cap, in a hex packing) is one of the most recognisable shapes there is. Most viewers will think 'pencils' within 2-3 s, so the uproot confirms a guess instead of surprising anyone. 'The landscape is actually a miniature object' is a well-worn tilt-shift and scale-reveal trope. Bundles of dancing colour pencils are common in stationery commercials, so the back half feels like a premium product ad rather than something crazy. The opening is slow: a 6 cm dolly over 5 s.

scores.title: THE DAWN WORKS
scores.strengths: The most emotional story and the strongest final image: rivers of light braid into a helix and ignite the sun, and the reveal that the machine manufactures dawn re-frames the whole film. The colour flood at 7.4 s and the rivers falling upward at 21 s are strong festival moments. Using light as geometry (emissive rivers, arrival-driven ignition of the flora) is clean and deterministic. The grace note of lamps clicking off is charming, and the one-control-property-per-shot pipeline is smart.
scores.weaknesses: Seven seconds of near-monochrome grey dishes at the start fails 'stop the scroll in 2 s' and 'great saturated colours' at the most important moment. Most of its imagery is borrowed. A white beam splitting through a prism is the Dark Side of the Moon cover. The bioluminescent mushroom canyon is Avatar. The ribbed brutalist 'cathedral of industry' is Blade Runner 2049 and Dune. Satellite-dish fields are Contact. Its 'cathedral' scale and reverent tone are also the closest of the five to the monument-reveal feel of a temple reel. Three heavy sets (dish plateau, hall with 120 pipe runs, canyon) plus glass and fake volumetrics make it the most likely to look half-finished.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft:
Winner: FLIPSIDE. Ideas worth grafting onto it:

1) MUSIC-LOCKED FRONTS (from NEEDLE DROP and RANGE). Analyse the real downloaded track with numpy to produce beats.json and a band-energy array. Use them to drive the flip-front speed and the per-tile flip timing, so every kick sends a visible flip ripple across the dunes and ocean. Add a beat_pulse GN input. This turns pretty glitter into precise motion design.

2) UNISON FLIP ON THE LAST BAR (from RANGE's jump, hang and slam). Before the lid shot, every visible tile flips at once, hangs for one frame at 90 degrees edge-on (the frame goes almost dark and graphic), then slams over to the other colour on the final hit. This is very shareable.

3) REPLACE OR DE-RISK THE EYE (from NEEDLE DROP's cymatic mandala). From orbit, colliding flip-fronts paint a perfect Chladni or Bessel cymatic mandala in tangerine, cobalt, magenta and pearl across the ocean face, pulsing to the bass. It is more original and premium than a cartoon eye. If the eye stays, build it from strict geometric arcs and A/B test it against the mandala.

4) EARLIER, CLEARER HOOK (from NEEDLE DROP's 4.2 s reveal timing). Start the crane-up by about 2.5 s instead of 3.5 s, and make the first flip happen within the first 12-18 frames so the hook lands in the first second.

5) A MOVING COLOUR FRONT AS THE STORY, PLUS REAL SPILL LIGHT (from THE DAWN WORKS). Hidden point and area lights ride each flip-front, so cobalt and magenta actually spill onto neighbouring tangerine tiles and the spray. One custom property per shot ('front', 'flock', 'planet') drives timing, so retiming to the music is trivial.

6) A CRISP TERMINATOR-LINE LOOK (from ONESIDE). Shoot the flip-front like ONESIDE's clock-hand shadow line: a razor-straight graphic boundary sweeping across the frame in a high wide shot. Also take the 'first wrong-physics hint' idea: a few loose sequins drift upward just before the front arrives.

7) HORIZON-CURVES-UP REVEAL (from ONESIDE's 'sky is land'). During the S5 pull-out, let the sequin horizon visibly bend into the planet curve sooner and more dramatically, a cheap but strong scale jolt.

8) SCALE GRAMMAR (from RANGE). Use deep focus, mist and wide lenses whenever something should read as kilometres, and shallow DOF with long lenses whenever it should read as millimetres. Switching DOF at the bead/lid shot sells the world-to-object flip.

9) AUDIO LOOP (from NEEDLE DROP and ONESIDE). Use the exact same tick or click SFX file at 0.0 s and at the end, and low-pass the music at the start, opening the filter fully on the crane-up reveal. Crossfade the music's final bar into the opening bar for a seamless social loop.

10) PIPELINE QA (from ONESIDE, NEEDLE DROP and DAWN WORKS):
- numerically difference frame 720 against frame 1
- use handoff.json velocity, heading and roll matching across hidden cuts
- do a 1280x720 low-sample previz of the full film before the overnight render to lock timing
- review a 12-frame-per-shot contact sheet
- render a 24-frame 50% strip specifically to check for glint shimmer

11) LAPTOP SAFETY, merged from all five (the user's explicit ask):
- check running blender.exe processes and free RAM before every launch, and queue rather than run in parallel if another Blender job is active
- run exactly one Blender process, at BelowNormal priority with -t 6
- have a watchdog pause if free RAM drops below about 12 GB, or abort a frame that exceeds 3x the benchmark time
- render in chunks, with overwrite off and placeholders on, and short thermal cool-downs between chunks
- watch for the iGPU TDR risk by testing the worst frame per shot first
- never realize instances
- keep textures at 2K or below
- run ffmpeg only after rendering finishes
- use unique output folders and never touch other jobs' files or processes

scores.title: RANGE
scores.strengths: Has the highest realistic quality ceiling of the five, because almost every frame uses materials EEVEE renders well under controlled light: clearcoat lacquer with orange-peel, object-space wave-texture growth rings, a matte pigment core, satin anodized metal, paper tooth and bone desk. There is one parametric hero mesh (smooth_min of hex and cone gives a real six-arc scallop with no booleans, about 50k and 6k tris at two LODs), instanced 288 times through Geometry Nodes, so all the polish goes into one asset. Memory and render time stay low: realistically 15-30 s per frame at 1440p. One world, one unit system and one continuous scale story mean very little set-building compared with the others. The beat-driven pencil 'dance' is a cheap GN height offset that looks crisp and deliberate. The DOF switch is used as storytelling: deep focus while the range reads as mountains, shallow at true scale. The shot-6 stroke that redraws the shot-1 skyline is a tight, satisfying loop. Lettering, dipped end cap and crumbs are cheap, legible hero detail. It contains nothing temple-like and no teal or gold.
scores.weaknesses: 1) The illusion may give itself away. A blond cedar cone with a coloured tip and a scalloped hex edge is one of the most recognisable silhouettes there is, and 288 near-identical 10-degree half-angle spikes on a hex grid read as pin-art, a hedgehog, or simply pencils, not mountains. Real peaks slope around 30 degrees; these slope around 80. 2) The geometry limits the 'range'. The cone is only about 2.1 cm long (0.375 / tan 10 degrees), so any height variation larger than that pushes painted hex bodies up through a single-height cloud slab. The fBm massifs therefore have to stay nearly flat, or the slab has to follow the terrain. 3) EEVEE volumetrics at clip-start 0.005 at macro scale risk froxel stepping and flicker at the slab boundary. Volume start/end must be tuned per shot, and the alpha-card fallback may well be needed. 4) Shot 4's 200x pull-back inside one scene risks a visible LOD pop, virtual-shadow-map swimming as the scale changes, and a drawn-out DOF ramp. 5) Shots 4-5 are a familiar product-viz image (coloured pencils in a cup) and a familiar pin-art wave, so the middle 10 s can feel like a stationery ad rather than 'crazy'. 6) The rigid-body crumbs are an unnecessary risk; use keyframed parabolas from the start.

scores.title: NEEDLE DROP
scores.strengths: Every set plays to procedural or EEVEE strengths. The turntable (Screw-modifier platter, knurled counterweight, strobe dots, bevel plus weighted normals, chrome under strip softboxes) is product-viz an AI can make truly premium. The wire tunnel is a pure GN helix. The city is GN instancing driven by a baked 32-band by 720-frame spectrum EXR, so motion locks to the music frame-accurately with no hand timing, which is the strongest 'top-tier motion studio' tool in any concept. The Bessel/Chladni cymatic desert (J_m(kr)cos(m theta) baked to an EXR, revealed by an expanding front) is a mathematically clean, very graphic image procedural tools do brilliantly, and the 700 m top-down reading as a record is a real payoff. Volumetrics are off everywhere and refraction appears on one object only. Hidden cuts on occluder frames, with velocity carried over through handoff.json, are good craft. The loop on the same crackle file is neat.
scores.weaknesses: 1) Six completely unrelated sets (groove, turntable, wire, city, cone, desert) is the largest build scope, and each needs its own look-dev pass in one night. 2) Several beats are known tropes: the fly-through inside a record groove, the audio-visualizer EQ city (Tron and visualizer-plugin territory), and the speaker-cone slam. The 'surprise' is a chain of clever transitions more than one jaw-drop. 3) Box cities are a classic procedural tell. Generic chamfered towers with window strips can look like a 2010 visualizer unless the rooftops and setbacks are dense. 4) Waveform-displaced groove walls at 60 m scale can read as wobbly candy rather than precision-cut vinyl. 5) The faceted diamond's raytraced refraction in EEVEE is screen-space and can look wrong (a fallback exists). 6) Fine concentric rings seen from altitude risk moiré: features must stay at least 6 px wide, and the mipmapping and blur have to be right. 7) Funky house plus a city of LEDs pulls the tone toward 'music promo' rather than 'cinematic'.

scores.title: FLIPSIDE
scores.strengths: The best underlying system of all five: one hex sequin mesh plus one GN group, in which a per-instance arrival time (dot(rest, front_dir)/speed + noise + rnd) drives a spring-overshoot flip curve. Every transformation (desert to ocean, flock, grove, eye) is the same deterministic math, with no simulation. Stable numpy point sets with a static per-shot frustum cull keep IDs and motion vectors stable, so EEVEE motion blur works. The two-sided colour trick (swap the stage only while a face points down, giving three states from two sides) is clever. The macro shots S1 and S6, with cupped bevelled tiles, centre holes and star glints, can look jewellery-commercial premium. The tangerine and cobalt palette is fresh and nothing like the reference. The S6 loop is solved backwards from S1's frame 0 and checked with a difference image.
scores.weaknesses: 1) Sub-pixel specular shimmer from 350-400k tilting metallic micro-mirrors under EEVEE's half-res screen-traced reflections and TAA is the top quality risk, and it shows as temporal sparkle noise that looks cheap, not luxurious. 2) The ocean will not read as water; it reads as a blue sequin carpet moving. 3) The near-instance to shader-faked far-field blend is a classic visible seam on a moving crane. 4) Six heavy subsystems (dunes, front plus 30k spray, 180k-tile murmuration with three blended phases, grove rebuild onto jacaranda samples, a 250k-tile planet with eye mask, loop) is enormous scope. 5) Sequin-skinned jacarandas and quiver trees risk looking like kitsch glitter sculptures. 6) The giant blinking eye risks looking cheesy, as the concept itself admits. 7) Thin-film iridescence may not be supported in EEVEE; the fallback is a fake. 8) Virtual shadow maps over hundreds of thousands of tiny casters, plus per-frame GN evaluation of complex murmuration math, push render time toward the top of the budget.

scores.title: THE DAWN WORKS
scores.strengths: Emissive-in-darkness is an EEVEE comfort zone: bloom on hot cores, raytraced colour spill onto wet basalt and concrete, and darkness that hides procedural flaws. The hard-surface pieces are excellent procedural targets: a GN field of about 400 Screw-modifier dishes turning in a delay wave, array-ribbed brutalist vaults, Bezier pipes with GN flanges and bolts, and radial-array turbine vats. Deterministic arrival-time ignition along rivers (Geometry Proximity to the channel U) is clean. One control property per shot ('front', 'split', 'rise', 'ignite') makes re-timing trivial. The monochrome-to-colour hit at 7.4 s is a strong emotional device, and the tiny lamps-off grace note is a lovely touch.
scores.weaknesses: 1) The first 7.4 s is deliberately grey, which goes directly against a brief that asks for 'great saturated colours'. A quarter of the film spent desaturated is a gamble with this client. 2) The ideas are familiar: a prism splitting light into a rainbow (Dark Side of the Moon), bioluminescent mushroom canyons (Avatar), rivers of neon light. It is poetic but not 'crazy'. 3) The weakest elements are organic and atmospheric, which is exactly where procedural work looks cheap: a cloud sea built as a displaced translucent mesh (cotton-wool tell without volumetrics), fake volumetric beam cones, flat emissive ribbon 'rivers' that read as neon tubes, and Poly Haven cliffs instanced along a spline with seams to hide. 4) Six shots across three full environments, plus a 4K macro trunk, plus a hero refractive prism, is large scope. 5) Dark gradients on an iGPU EEVEE render raise banding and noise risk. 6) Electric Cyan sits close to the banned teal.

scores.title: ONESIDE
scores.strengths: The most conceptually 'crazy' world: sky made of land, sunset caused by the ground rolling over, a river wrapping the rim, day and night as places. The single map(s, v, h) source of truth for the terrain, rail, train, camera and scatter is good engineering. Camera paths defined in the ribbon's own coordinates and baked through map() keep everything in sync. The corkscrew shot (camera locked to the train while the world rolls, with a fixed sun so the lighting change is physically free) is a genuinely great image idea. Scatter is computed once per shot from the whole camera path, so nothing pops.
scores.weaknesses: 1) Its beauty depends on naturalistic landscape fidelity (grass-blade-height meadows, recoloured Poly Haven flowers and jacarandas, noise-terraced mesas), which is the domain where AI-procedural EEVEE work most reliably looks like a cheap CG game level. 2) 1.5-2M grass instances at 0.35 m in EEVEE on a 780M make S1 and S6 the heaviest, slowest shots of any concept. 3) The rim-wrap water is curve-to-mesh with scrolling streaks and no simulation, a textbook cheap tell, and it sits at the key surprise moment. 4) Thickened-Möbius slab math (two faces meeting at a seam, normals flipping, terrain continuity under periodic 4D noise) is the highest engineering risk, and any error shows in the 5 km reveal. 5) A whole-world reveal of a 1.3 km ribbon with sparse trees reads as a toy diorama. 6) A beveled-cube-plus-lattice maglev will look generic. 7) A night bioluminescent forest needing about 40 point lights, plus day/night world keying in sync with the roll, is a lot of fragile look-dev. 8) 'Recoloured Poly Haven jacaranda' is an off-palette asset forced into the palette.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft:
Winner: RANGE. Grafts, in priority order:

1) FLIPSIDE's arrival-time and spring system for 'The Range Plays' and the tremor. Instead of plain sine ripples, give each pencil an arrival time (radial distance / speed + noise + rnd) and drive its Z with a spring-overshoot Float Curve (0, 1.08, 0.97, 1). Every beat launches a front with crisp settle-wobble per pencil. It looks far more premium than sine waves at the same cost. Also use it for the shot-3 tremor: a ripple of micro-jumps outward from the crimson pencil before it uproots.

2) NEEDLE DROP's audio-analysis pipeline. Bake a 32-band by 720-frame spectrum EXR plus beats.json from the real downloaded track, and map hex rings from the centre outward to frequency bands (bass in the inner rings, highs on the rim). The drum then becomes a literal EQ, with no hand-keyed timing. Also take its music filter automation: low-pass or airy treatment during the 'mountain' shots, sweeping fully open at the studio reveal, as an audio cue for the scale change.

3) Fixes for the illusion: keep the pencil height variance below the cone length (about 2.1 cm), or make the cloud slab or alpha cards follow the local height field so no painted hex body shows before shot 3. Use more worn, broken and blunt tips and varied cone angles (sharpener variants of 14-22 degrees) so the field does not read as pin-art.

4) NEEDLE DROP's subliminal scale clue (the lint fibre bridging the canyon) and 'shadow arrives before the giant object'. In shot 2, a single giant paper fibre or eraser crumb arcs across the 'sky' as a clue that only lands on rewatch. In shot 6, the crimson pencil's shadow sweeps across the paper before the tip enters frame.

5) FLIPSIDE's stable-ID discipline: numpy-built point sets, a per-shot static frustum cull, and scale-to-zero instead of deleting points, so EEVEE motion blur never breaks on the dancing pencils or crumbs. Also its roughness floor of 0.12 or more on lacquer and foil to prevent glint fireflies and shimmer, the star-streak Glare on lacquer highlights, and Light Path 'Is Camera Ray' to light from a studio HDRI while the camera sees the procedural gradient sweep.

6) DAWN WORKS' one-control-property-per-shot rule (for example 'uproot', 'pull', 'wave', 'stroke', all read by GN and shaders), so re-timing to the final music edit is a one-line change. Also its full-film 1280x720 low-sample previz pass to lock sync before the overnight render, and hidden animated lights that follow moving highlights.

7) NEEDLE DROP's handoff.json velocity and heading matching across cuts, and cutting on occluder frames (the rising tower filling frame at 15.0 s, the void top-down).

8) ONESIDE's camera-locked-to-hero trick for shot 3: for part of the uproot, lock the camera to the rising crimson tower so the whole range drops away around a steady subject. Also its single parametric source of truth: define the shot-1 skyline curve once and reuse it for the shot-6 stroke so the loop matches exactly. Verify the loop with FLIPSIDE's frame difference image.

9) Laptop safety, combined from all concepts since the user explicitly asked for it. Before each launch, check tasklist for blender.exe and free RAM, and queue rather than run in parallel. Run only one Blender process from this pipeline, at BelowNormal priority, with -t 6 to 8. Use a free-RAM floor of about 12-20 GB, a watchdog that aborts a frame taking more than 3x the benchmark (DAWN WORKS), 24-50 frame chunks with Overwrite off and Placeholders on, and cool-downs between chunks. Run ffmpeg only after all rendering finishes, use 2K textures at most, never realize instances, keep a unique output folder, and never touch or kill other jobs.

scores.title: RANGE
scores.strengths: The camera grammar does the storytelling. Shots 1-3 use deep focus, wide lenses (16-28mm), a mist pass and a hard 4-degree sun, so the range reads as kilometres. Shots 4-6 ramp to f/2.8 with 70-100mm lenses and soft studio light, so it reads as centimetres. The DOF ramp during the single exponential pull-back is the best cinematography idea in the batch, because the lens itself does the scale reveal. The shot lengths (5 / 4.5 / 5.5 / 5.5 / 5 / 4.5 s) give an even, breathing rhythm. The uproot shot has strong film language: a 16mm locked-off shot with decaying shake, a 70-degree tilt-up with lag for weight, and motion blur smearing the foil lettering. The edit map is very clear: ambient intro, riser 9.5-14, a half-beat silence at 14.5, a sub-boom hard cut at 15.0, the drop at 20.5, and a button at 29.3. The sound design has the strongest scale illusion of the five. A wooden creak pitched down and layered with stone grinding turns a pencil into a mountain by ear. The pencil clatter cut onto downbeats, the unison jump and slam, and the intimate scratch on paper after the drums give real dynamic contrast. The beat-driven GN wave keys off beats.json from the actual edit, so picture and sound stay locked. Colour is disciplined: 24 pigments against neutral cedar, paper and navy. It is the most buildable concept, with one object repeated 288 times, and the most likely to look clean.
scores.weaknesses: The hook is weak. Nothing happens for 10.8 s: two slow establishing shots and a dolly that travels about 6 cm. A 30 s social piece needs an event or a hint by about 3 s. 'Everyday object as landscape' is a well-worn trope (macro-landscape photography, stationery ads), so part of the audience will guess 'crayons/pencils' early. Six-sided cones with painted scallops are very recognisable. If the volume cloud slab flickers or reads thin in EEVEE, shot 1 gives the reveal away. The studio reveal (16-19 s) is a third reveal stacked on the first and partly dilutes it. The 'range plays the music' section risks reading as a cute audio-visualiser rather than a climax. It needs one composition change mid-section, not just a 60-degree orbit. The music is very hard to source: one real track needs an ambient intro, a riser, a clean gap and a playful pizzicato groove at exact times. It will almost certainly be two tracks spliced, and the tonal jump from epic to playful at 20.5 s can feel like a different film. The shot 4 continuous LOD switch over a 200x scale change is the hardest single shot to make seamless.

scores.title: FLIPSIDE
scores.strengths: It is the most original material idea: one two-sided sequin that becomes desert, ocean, flock, forest, planet and eye. The front-riding shot in S3 is a superb graphic frame: camera parallel to a moving transformation front, tangerine desert on the left, cobalt ocean on the right, spray between. The 100-to-32mm partial dolly-zoom crane-up is good scale language. The murmuration diving over the lens with a 50-to-18mm lens change and a roll is a strong kinetic moment. The tangerine/cobalt complementary pair is maximally punchy. The tactile SFX palette is excellent and very premium: single sequin tick, receding domino rattle, slowed rain stick, beads poured on a table, glass-chime splash, wing flutter layered with shakers. Ending on a final tick that matches the 1.8 s click is a good audio loop. The spring-overshoot flip and per-tile arrival times give every wave texture.
scores.weaknesses: It is overstuffed. Seven transformations in 30 s leave no beat to land, and the drop at 8.5 s spends the big energy early, so the remaining 21 s must keep escalating with no breather. Every frame is the same micro-texture (glittering hex tiles), so there is little variety in light and material; after 10 s it can read as a 'glitter shader on everything' filter. 'Clean as hell' is the biggest problem. Hundreds of thousands of tiny mirror facets at 1440p in EEVEE will crawl and shimmer temporally. Glitter fields are also the worst case for codecs: H.264/H.265 and Instagram/YouTube re-compression will turn it into macroblocked mush, which undoes the premium look. Star-streak glare on thousands of glints adds visual noise. The giant blinking eye is a tonal swerve toward cartoon and risks cheese. The macro opening reads as abstract glitter with no anchor, which makes a weak hook. It is the most complex build (180k rank-matched flock, Gerstner sequins, planet eye, frustum culling), so the risk of half-finished shots is highest. The music brief is generic: 'future bass with sparkle'.

scores.title: ONESIDE
scores.strengths: It has the single best camera idea of the five: the S2 corkscrew. The camera is locked to the train's reference frame, so the whole world rolls 180 degrees around a steady subject, the sun sets under the ground, and the terminator sweeps the canyon like a clock hand. It is physically motivated light change done entirely by camera, and very cinematic. The 'over the rim' continuous 180-degree camera roll following the water is a second excellent move. The +1.3 EV glare white-out hides the cut honestly. The 'sky is land' crane-up is a classic, effective reveal. The 7 s pull-out to the whole Möbius ribbon, half day and half night, gives the film one held, breathing wide. The maglev hum rising under the loop point is good continuity sound design.
scores.weaknesses: The material is the weakest category for procedural AI building: organic landscapes. A grass meadow at 0.35 m and f/2, plus Poly Haven flowers, jacarandas, a river and night ferns, tends to look like an asset-store or game environment, not a premium studio piece. The 'land overhead' Ringworld/Inception image and the Möbius strip floating in a nebula are familiar sci-fi pictures. A 1.3 km ribbon framed at 5.5 km can read as a toy. Music integration is the weakest of the five: a generic 'hybrid strings plus arpeggio' track with three sync points. Nothing on screen moves to the beat, so the edit is a ride with music underneath, not cut to it. The SFX are conventional (doppler pass-by, crickets, waterfall roar, space drone). Water without a sim, wrapping a rim in a hero close-up, will look like a scrolling texture. The maglev design (bevelled box) is generic. The scope is very wide: meadow, corkscrew canyon, night forest, rim, space and boulder belt are six environments plus Möbius maths. The 'seamless loop' device is shared with three other concepts, so it is no longer a differentiator.

scores.title: THE DAWN WORKS
scores.strengths: It has the strongest light-as-story arc. A strict near-monochrome first 7.4 s, then a prism split floods the screen with saturated colour on a key hit. The Act 2 world is lit only by its emitters, then the backlight comes from a sun the world has just made. The colour carries the narrative throughout (beam, then vats, then rivers, then fungi, then sky, then sun), so the eye always has a moving front to follow. The cause-and-effect story is the clearest and most emotional. Editorially it is well built around three downbeats (7.4, 21.0, 27.5). The 'suck-out' silence or reverse-cymbal pull at 20.8 before the 21.0 hit is textbook trailer craft. It has the richest SFX plan: staggered servo whirs, filament zaps, a sluice CLANK, seven turbine spin-ups panned across the stereo field. The grace note of three tiny relay clicks as lamps go off after the big sun hit gives the ending a human-scale button. The production idea of one control property per shot ('front', 'split', 'rise', 'ignite') is smart for retiming.
scores.weaknesses: The visual ingredients are the most derivative of the five: a Dark Side of the Moon prism, an Avatar bioluminescent mushroom forest, glowing magic ribbons in the sky, a brutalist sci-fi factory. It surprises in story, not in image, and the brief asks for 'crazy'. The grey first 7 s fights the brief's 'great saturated colours' for a quarter of the runtime. A slow 70-90 BPM orchestral build means trailer grammar with few cuts and no groove, closer to an epic game cinematic than a motion-design showcase. Emissive-only scenes in EEVEE easily become 'glow soup' with bloom haloes and flat neon ribbons. Liquid light without a fluid sim, and a displaced-mesh cloud sea without volumes, both risk looking plasticky. 'Falling upward' lands softer than intended because the rivers are already light, not water, so breaking gravity is less shocking. The scope is six distinct sets including a detailed brutalist hall.

scores.title: NEEDLE DROP
scores.strengths: It is the only concept where the soundtrack is the protagonist, which suits the brief's music requirement best. The groove walls are the waveform, the city towers are FFT bands, the cone excursion is the bass envelope, and the desert becomes a cymatic record. Every motion is data-locked to the real edited track (spectrum.exr plus beats.json), so it will feel frame-accurately in sync in a way hand keys never do. Its sound design as POV is brilliant and cheap: the music is low-passed at 700 Hz 'inside the groove', opens up fully on the 6.0 s reveal, is band-passed inside the wire, and gets a wide reverb tail in the desert. That is real editorial storytelling done with filters on licensed audio. It plays as one continuous signal-chain ride, with handoff.json matching velocity, heading and roll across hidden cuts, which is sophisticated continuity. The ending payoff is the best of the five: the tonearm shadow arrives first, then a colossal arm lowers onto a desert that has become a record, and the film cuts to black on the same needle-drop crackle that opened it. That is a perfect audio loop. A nu-disco or future-funk groove at about 120 BPM gives the energy 'crazy' needs. The turntable product shot will look unmistakably premium in EEVEE.
scores.weaknesses: It is relentless. Five high-speed FPV or flythrough moves with almost no held frame mean no breath and no contrast, so the drop at 22.5 s has less to land against. Every transition is the same 'fly into hole / occluder wipe' (cantilever, RCA bore, white-out, hex grille, cone face). Five identical wipes in 30 s become a gimmick; it needs at least one hard smash cut. The EQ-bars-as-skyline city and the 'travel through the wire' tunnel are music-video and ad clichés. The 3 s wire shot is filler. The 'walls are the real waveform' detail is invisible at 30 m/s and 24 fps, so the concept's cleverness partly lives off-screen. Building six sets at about 5 s each spreads quality thin. A fine cymatic-ring desert seen from 700 m risks moiré, and a dense city of LED window strips risks aliasing and codec mush. The track must be chosen before any animation exists, which puts the music on the critical path.

judgements.best_ideas_to_graft:
1. Lens and DOF as the scale switch (RANGE). Wide lenses, deep focus, mist and a hard low sun read as kilometres. Long lenses, shallow DOF and soft studio light read as centimetres. Ramp f-stop and focal length inside the one continuous pull-back so the lens performs the reveal. Use this on any winner that has a scale flip.

2. Audio filter automation as point of view (NEEDLE DROP). Low-pass the licensed music while we are 'inside' or tiny, and sweep it fully open on the reveal frame. Use band-pass and reverb changes per world. It is pure editing on real recordings, cheap, and makes every reveal hit harder. In RANGE: muffled, distant music during the 'mountain' section, then the filter snaps open on the 15.0 s cut or the studio reveal.

3. Sell scale with pitch (RANGE). Pitch real small-object foley down (wooden creak, friction groan) and layer it with stone grinding so a small object sounds colossal. Then reverse it at the end: play the same object's true-pitch foley (scratch, tap, clatter) close-miked once the true scale is known.

4. Silence before the hit (RANGE's half-beat gap at 14.5 s; THE DAWN WORKS' suck-out at 20.8 s). Cut all audio, or use a reverse-cymbal pull, for 6-12 frames before the biggest picture event. Pair it with a hard cut on the hit, not a wipe.

5. All motion driven by data from the final audio edit (NEEDLE DROP, RANGE). Run numpy onset, beat and band-envelope analysis on the edited WAV, save it to beats.json and a per-frame band EXR, and read those in GN. Any music retime then updates the picture automatically. Add attack/release smoothing and a per-frame clamp so nothing strobes at 24 fps.

6. One control property per shot (THE DAWN WORKS: 'front', 'split', 'rise', 'ignite'), read by GN and shaders, so timing lives in one keyed curve.

7. Hand off camera velocity across cuts (NEEDLE DROP). Each shot writes its last-frame velocity, heading and roll to handoff.json, and the next shot seeds its path from it. On-screen motion then flows across cuts. Vary the transitions, though: no more than two occluder wipes, with the rest as hard cuts on beats.

8. Hint in the first 3 seconds (FLIPSIDE's 2.4 s 'something is coming' domino line). RANGE's slow 10 s opening needs an early event. For example, the sunrise could ignite the pigment summits one by one at about 1-4 s, each on a pluck or chime (this also borrows DAWN WORKS' 'colour arrives' idea). Or a small crumb rockslide at about 3 s could foreshadow the tremor.

9. Colour arriving as a travelling front (THE DAWN WORKS, FLIPSIDE). Start desaturated or pre-dawn and let saturation sweep across the frame on the first musical hit. FLIPSIDE's per-instance 'arrival time' attribute with a spring-overshoot response is the right tool, and it would also give RANGE's dancing range a directional ripple front instead of a uniform pump.

10. Lock the camera to the hero so the world moves (ONESIDE's corkscrew). Parent the camera to the moving subject with zero relative roll and let the environment rotate around it. A sun terminator line sweeping across the terrain is a free, physically correct light change. It fits RANGE's uprooting pencil: lock the camera to the rising pencil so the whole range drops away.

11. Riding-the-front split composition (FLIPSIDE). Track parallel to a moving transformation front with the 'before' world on one side of frame and the 'after' world on the other. It is a strong graphic frame for any transformation beat.

12. The shadow arrives before the giant (NEEDLE DROP). A huge shadow crosses the frame before the colossal object enters. In RANGE's last shot, the crimson pencil's shadow should sweep across the paper before the tip enters frame.

13. Glare white-out to hide a cut (ONESIDE: +1.3 EV with a glare ramp over 0.6 s). Use it as one of the varied transition types.

14. A quiet button after the big hit (THE DAWN WORKS: lamps blink off with tiny relay clicks). After the final music hit, add one small, intimate sound-and-picture beat before black. For RANGE: one crumb settles, or the pencil is set down with a soft wooden tick.

15. Loop by reusing the exact opening SFX file at the end (NEEDLE DROP's needle-drop crackle, FLIPSIDE's tick at 1.8 s and 29.9 s). It makes a social-media loop seamless by ear even if the picture match is imperfect.

16. Hidden lights riding emissive fronts (THE DAWN WORKS). Animate real area or point lights along with every emissive event so EEVEE gets genuine colour spill and does not rely on emissive GI.

17. Plan the finish for compression. Avoid frame-filling sub-pixel glitter or grass, keep a roughness floor of at least 0.12, keep fine repeating detail at 6 px or more on screen, add light grain before encoding, and deliver at high bitrate. FLIPSIDE's frustum-culled fixed point sets (stable IDs, so motion blur works and nothing pops) are worth reusing for any instanced field.

18. Tactile real-world SFX sources (FLIPSIDE). Use beads poured on a table, slowed rain stick, glass chimes and shakers as the 'texture' layer under any mass-instancing animation. In RANGE: wooden sticks and pencils clattering in a cup, cut to the beat.
